463.title: Here am I (Isaiah 6:1–8)
463.hook: Isaiah sees the Lord high and lifted up, and says here am I, send me
463.howItsDone: Christians sing the seraphim's 'Holy, holy, holy' in the Sanctus of the communion service, and Isaiah 6 is often read at ordinations and when people are commissioned for mission or service.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the prophets began with Nathan's thou art the man, and your line: truth to power.

It begins with a date: "In the year that king Uzziah died." A king is dead, and a whole kingdom is waiting to see what comes next. In that year, a man named Isaiah is in the Temple in Jerusalem, and he sees something. The Lord, sitting on a throne, high and lifted up, the hem of his robe filling the whole Temple. Above him, beings with six wings each, calling to one another. The doorposts shake. The house fills with smoke.
screen: `THE YEAR KING UZZIAH DIED.` → `A THRONE, HIGH AND LIFTED UP.` → `THE DOORPOSTS SHAKE.`

segments.voice: The text calls these beings seraphim, a name some readers link to a Hebrew word for burning. With two wings they cover their faces, with two their feet, and with two they fly, and they call: "Holy, holy, holy, is the LORD of hosts: the whole earth is full of his glory." Churches still sing that line in the Sanctus at communion, and in hymns. Isaiah's first reaction isn't wonder. It's terror: "Woe is me! for I am undone; because I am a man of unclean lips." Not terrible deeds: an unclean mouth, the very thing a prophet needs. Then one of the seraphim flies to the altar, takes a live coal with tongs, and touches it to his lips. Your guilt is taken away, it says. Now, at last, a question from the throne, and it isn't a command: "Whom shall I send, and who will go for us?" And Isaiah: "Here am I; send me." In Hebrew that's hineni, one short word: here I am. Abraham says it when God calls him, Moses at the burning bush, the boy Samuel in the night. It doesn't mean I'm qualified; Isaiah has just said he isn't. It means present, listening, available. And it comes before he knows the job. The next verses give him a hard message for a people who won't listen. He says yes first. Christians hear their own calls in this scene at ordinations and sendings for mission, and in ordinary moments too: someone asks who will go, and a hand goes up.
screen: `HOLY, HOLY, HOLY.` · `WOE IS ME: UNCLEAN LIPS.` · `A LIVE COAL ON THE MOUTH.` · `HINENI: HERE I AM.` · then, large: `HERE AM I; SEND ME.`

segments.voice: Notice where you are right now, the chair, the room, the sounds, the light, and let yourself be fully here, the way hineni means. Then think of one place this week where someone is asking, in their own way, who will go, a neighbor, a coworker, a family member, a cause, and simply turn toward it; you don't have to fix it. If you pray, you can say Isaiah's words, here am I, send me; if you don't, simply say here I am, and mean it.
Hineni. Hebrew for here I am, the answer of Abraham, Moses, Samuel and Isaiah, said present and available, before any of them knew the job.
Your line: send me. Present first, and the job comes after that. See you tomorrow.

464.title: Swords into ploughshares (Isaiah 2:2–4)
464.hook: the nations will beat swords into ploughshares and learn war no more
464.howItsDone: Isaiah 2:4 is often read in Advent and at services of prayer for peace; the phrase study war no more comes from the African American spiritual Down by the Riverside, sung in churches and at peace gatherings.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Isaiah in the Temple, hineni, here I am, and your line: send me.

In the garden of the United Nations in New York stands a bronze statue of a muscular man. He holds a hammer high over his head. In his other hand is a sword, and he's bending its blade; the end is already curling into the shape of a plow. The statue was a gift from the Soviet Union, during the Cold War, while both sides were building bombs. Its title comes from an old Hebrew prophet, writing in a small kingdom squeezed between empires.
screen: `A STATUE AT THE UNITED NATIONS.` → `A HAMMER OVER A SWORD.` → `THE BLADE BECOMING A PLOW.`

segments.voice: Isaiah, chapter two, sees a day to come: the mountain of the Lord's house raised above the hills, and all nations streaming to it. Not dragged. Streaming, like a river running uphill, saying, let's go up, so he'll teach us his ways. Then, in the King James Bible: "and they shall beat their swords into plowshares, and their spears into pruninghooks: nation shall not lift up sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more." Take it literally. A plowshare is the iron blade that cuts the soil; a pruning hook trims vines. Iron was precious, so you didn't bury or hide it. You reforged it. The same metal that killed now feeds. And the last phrase: they shall not learn war any more. War is something learned, so it can be unlearned. The same vision appears almost word for word in the prophet Micah, who adds that everyone will sit under their own vine and fig tree, with no one to make them afraid. The prophet Joel turns the image around, calling people to beat their plowshares into swords for battle. The Bible knows both directions; Isaiah's points to the end of the story. Christians often read it as a promise of God's kingdom, and hear Jesus' blessing on the peacemakers as a call to live toward it now. Some, Mennonites and Quakers among them, take it as a call to refuse war entirely. Others hold it as the goal while believing defense can be just. And an old African American spiritual, Down by the Riverside, carries the last phrase into song: study war no more.

segments.voice: Think of one small weapon you carry, a sharp tone, a grudge you sharpen, a habit of winning arguments, a post you keep meaning to write, and hold it in your mind like a piece of iron. Picture the hammer, and the blade slowly becoming a tool: a conversation instead of a jab, help instead of a grudge. If you pray, you can pray for peace in one place you know of, by name.

465.title: Unto us a child (Isaiah 9:2–7)
465.hook: the people who walked in darkness have seen a great light
465.howItsDone: Isaiah 9:2–7 is one of the most common readings at Christmas services, including the traditional service of lessons and carols, and many Christians light candles through Advent while waiting for Christmas.

segments.voice: Yesterday, swords into plowshares, the pruninghook, and your line: study war no more.

In December, in concert halls and churches in many countries, a choir waits for a particular chorus. The violins start running, light and quick. Then the whole choir lands, all together, on a string of names, hammered out one at a time. Handel wrote it in London, and it was first heard in Dublin in 1742. But the words weren't his. They come from the prophet Isaiah, written more than seven centuries before Jesus, to a kingdom with an army on its border.
screen: `A CHOIR WAITS IN DECEMBER.` → `A STRING OF NAMES, HAMMERED OUT.` → `THE WORDS ARE ISAIAH'S.`

segments.voice: Isaiah's world was dark in a literal way. The Assyrian empire was on the march, and the northern lands of Zebulun and Naphtali, up around the Sea of Galilee, were among the first to be overrun. Into that, Isaiah says, in the King James Bible: "The people that walked in darkness have seen a great light: they that dwell in the land of the shadow of death, upon them hath the light shined." Notice the tense. Have seen: the rescue spoken of as if it's already happened. Then he names the light: "For unto us a child is born, unto us a son is given: and the government shall be upon his shoulder: and his name shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, The mighty God, The everlasting Father, The Prince of Peace." Not a general. Not a weapon. A baby. The soldiers' boots, Isaiah says, will be burned as fuel for the fire, and this child's peace will have no end, on the throne of David. Who is the child? Here readers differ. Many Jewish readers have understood it as a royal child of Isaiah's own time, often King Hezekiah, or as a future king of David's line. Christians, from the Gospels on, read it as Jesus. Matthew's Gospel quotes this very passage when Jesus begins preaching in Galilee, the land of Zebulun and Naphtali, the first place the darkness fell. For Christians, the light rose exactly where the shadow had begun. That's why these words come back every Christmas: a child, given, into a dark place.

segments.voice: If you can, light a real candle and set it in front of you; if not, picture one clearly, and notice how small the flame is, and how much of the room it changes. Then think of one dark place you know about right now, a family going through something, a city in the news, a corner of your own life, and hold the flame and that place together in your mind. If you pray, you can pray for that place by name.

Your line: a great light. Even a small flame changes a room. See you tomorrow.

466.title: The wolf and the lamb (Isaiah 11:1–9)
466.hook: a shoot from a stump, and a little child will lead them
466.howItsDone: Isaiah 11 is often read during Advent, and some families and congregations make a Jesse tree, hanging ornaments for the stories of Jesus's ancestors; the Quaker painter Edward Hicks painted this vision as The Peaceable Kingdom.

segments.voice: Yesterday, unto us a child, Wonderful Counsellor, and your line: a great light.

A forest a few years after the loggers have gone: stumps everywhere, flat, gray, finished. But look closer. Out of the side of an old stump, a thin green shoot with two or three leaves. The tree was cut down. The roots weren't. Isaiah had watched the royal family of David shrink and fail: kings who trusted armies instead of God, a kingdom being cut down to the ground. And from that stump, he saw something growing.
screen: `A FOREST OF STUMPS.` → `A GREEN SHOOT FROM THE SIDE.` → `DAVID'S LINE, CUT DOWN.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots." Jesse was David's father. Some readers hear in that a return past David, to the roots, before the kings went wrong. On this new shoot, Isaiah says, the spirit of the Lord will rest: wisdom, understanding, counsel, might, knowledge, the fear of the Lord. This king won't judge by what his eyes see or his ears hear. He'll judge the poor with fairness. Then the picture everyone remembers: "The wolf also shall dwell with the lamb, and the leopard shall lie down with the kid; and the calf and the young lion and the fatling together; and a little child shall lead them." Every pair is a predator and its dinner. A baby plays at the hole of a snake. The world's whole food chain, the logic of eat or be eaten, stops. And who's in charge? Not a lion. A little child, leading. One slip worth catching: people sometimes quote it as the lion shall lie down with the lamb. The text never says that. It's the wolf that dwells with the lamb, the leopard that lies down with the kid. The vision ends: "They shall not hurt nor destroy in all my holy mountain." Christians read the shoot of Jesse as Jesus, and some churches hang a Jesse tree in Advent, tracing his family. Jewish tradition reads it as the hope of a messiah still to come. Both keep the picture of a world where nothing preys on anything.

segments.voice: Think of something in your life that feels cut down, a friendship that ended, a plan that failed, a part of you that went quiet, and picture it as a stump. Let your attention rest on it without demanding it be a tree yet, and if you pray, give thanks for it.

Your line: a little child shall lead. The tree was cut, but not the roots. That's day four hundred sixty-six.

467.title: Comfort ye (Isaiah 40:1–11)
467.hook: speak tenderly; every valley lifted; he gathers the lambs in his arms
467.howItsDone: Christians read Isaiah 40 in Advent, often alongside the story of John the Baptist, and Handel's Messiah opens with it; in Jewish practice it is the prophetic reading on Shabbat Nachamu, the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the shoot from Jesse's stump, and your line: a little child shall lead.

Read Isaiah straight through and something happens at chapter forty. Chapter after chapter has been warnings, judgments and armies. Assyria is coming. Jerusalem is in danger. The chapter just before ends with a warning that the king's treasures, and his sons, will one day be carried off to Babylon. Then you turn the page, and the voice changes. Now it speaks to a city whose hard service is over, and to a people who need a road home. And the first word God speaks to them isn't a rebuke, or an explanation, or a lesson about what went wrong.
screen: `CHAPTER AFTER CHAPTER OF WARNING.` → `TURN THE PAGE.` → `CARRIED OFF TO BABYLON.` → `THE FIRST WORD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "Comfort ye, comfort ye my people, saith your God." Said twice, the way you'd say it to someone crying: it's okay, it's okay. In Hebrew it's nachamu, nachamu ammi. Then: "Speak ye comfortably to Jerusalem." Literally, speak to the heart of Jerusalem: the phrase used elsewhere in the Bible for someone wooing, or reassuring, someone they love. Tell her, God says, that her hard service is over. Then a voice cries out: make a road through the wilderness for God. "Every valley shall be exalted, and every mountain and hill shall be made low: and the crooked shall be made straight, and the rough places plain." Road builders filling every dip and leveling every hill, so God can come straight to his people and bring them home. People are like grass, the chapter reminds them; the grass withers, but God's word stands. And it ends tenderly: "He shall feed his flock like a shepherd: he shall gather the lambs with his arm, and carry them in his bosom, and shall gently lead those that are with young." Not driving the flock. Carrying the smallest, walking slowly for the mothers. Some scholars think this chapter begins a new part of the book, written later for the exiles; others hold the whole book to be Isaiah's. Christians hear the voice in the wilderness as John the Baptist, as all four Gospels say. And Jewish communities read this chapter on the Sabbath after Tisha B'Av, the fast that mourns the Temple: they call it the Sabbath of comfort.

468.title: Wings like eagles (Isaiah 40:28–31)
468.hook: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength
468.howItsDone: Christians often memorize Isaiah 40:31, and it is frequently read at funerals and shared with people facing illness or exhaustion; it also appears in many hymns and worship songs.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the first word of comfort, and your line: comfort ye my people.

It's mile twenty of a marathon. The crowds have thinned out. Legs that felt light at the start now feel like wet sand. Runners call it the wall, and even the young, fit ones hit it. Now stretch that wall across years instead of miles. That's where the people Isaiah speaks to are: worn down by a long, long wait for something to change. Some are saying out loud that God has forgotten them, that their cause has slipped past his notice. The same chapter that opened with comfort ends by answering them.
screen: `MILE TWENTY. THE WALL.` → `A LONG, LONG WAIT.` → `HAS GOD FORGOTTEN US?`

segments.voice: First the prophet asks, almost impatient: "Hast thou not known? hast thou not heard, that the everlasting God, the LORD, the Creator of the ends of the earth, fainteth not, neither is weary?" The one who made everything doesn't run out, and he gives power to the faint. Even young people get tired, Isaiah says; even strong young men stumble and fall. Strength isn't a matter of being young or fit. Then the line people have stitched onto pillows and painted on locker-room walls: "But they that wait upon the LORD shall renew their strength; they shall mount up with wings as eagles; they shall run, and not be weary; and they shall walk, and not faint." Two things to notice. First, wait. The Hebrew word leans toward hope; some translations render it those who hope in the Lord. It isn't sitting idle. It's leaning toward God, the way you lean toward a door when you hear the car pull in. Second, renew. The Hebrew verb can also mean to change or exchange, and some readers hear a trade: spent strength for new. And look at the order: fly, then run, then walk. It goes down, not up. You might expect the big finish to be soaring. Instead it ends with walking and not fainting. Some readers call that the honest part. Some days soar. Some days run. And plenty of days, the gift is to walk and not faint. That may be why people carry this verse into hospital rooms and funerals: it doesn't promise flying every day.
screen: `THE CREATOR FAINTETH NOT.` · `WAIT: LEANING TOWARD GOD.` · `RENEW: A TRADE OF STRENGTH.` · `FLY, RUN, WALK: IT GOES DOWN.` · then, large: `THEY SHALL MOUNT UP WITH WINGS AS EAGLES.`

segments.voice: Let your body be heavy, shoulders dropped, hands loose, feet flat, and notice where you're tired, your eyes, your back, your heart, without pushing past it. Then simply wait, leaning toward God or toward stillness, expecting nothing in particular, breathing out the spent strength and breathing in as if trading it for new. If you pray, you can say the line slowly: they that wait upon the Lord shall renew their strength.
Nesher. Hebrew for the great bird translated eagle, Isaiah's promise to the tired: those who wait on God exchange their strength, and soar, and run, and keep walking.
Your line: fly, then run, then walk. On the slow days, walking counts. See you tomorrow.

469.title: Called by name (Isaiah 43:1–3)
469.hook: fear not, I have called you by name; when you pass through the waters
469.howItsDone: Isaiah 43:1–3 is often read at Christian baptisms and confirmations, and Christians turn to it in times of fear or illness; it is also set in hymns and songs used in worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday, nesher, wings like eagles, and your line: fly, then run, then walk.

A crowded airport. Hundreds of people, announcements in three languages, nobody looking at anybody. Then, over the noise, someone calls out your name. Not excuse me. Not sir or ma'am. Your name. And you turn, instantly, before you've even thought about it. A name cuts through. The exiles Isaiah speaks to were a small, defeated people inside a great empire, easy to lose in the crowd: unseen, overlooked, swallowed. Isaiah has comforted them and promised them strength. Now he says something even more personal.
screen: `A CROWDED AIRPORT.` → `SOMEONE CALLS YOUR NAME.` → `EXILES, LOST IN THE CROWD.`

segments.voice: In the King James Bible: "But now thus saith the LORD that created thee, O Jacob, and he that formed thee, O Israel, Fear not: for I have redeemed thee, I have called thee by thy name; thou art mine." Notice the verbs. Created. Formed: a potter's word, the same one used when God shapes the first human from the dust in Genesis. Redeemed: the word for a family member who buys back a relative sold into debt, or buys back the family land. Then called by name. Then three words: thou art mine. Not a possession, the way you own a phone. Belonging, the way a child belongs to a family. Then the promise, with water and fire: "When thou passest through the waters, I will be with thee; and through the rivers, they shall not overflow thee: when thou walkest through the fire, thou shalt not be burned." It doesn't say you'll never pass through the waters. It says when. The flood and the fire are assumed. What's promised is company in them, and that they won't sweep you away. These words were first spoken to a whole people, Jacob and Israel, and Jewish readers hear them that way. Christians also hear them personally, and some churches read them at baptisms, where someone is named and passes through the water. This week in the prophets: hineni, pruninghook, Wonderful Counsellor, Branch, comfort ye, nesher, and today, Jacob. A week that moved from a prophet saying send me to God saying you are mine.
screen: `CREATED, FORMED, REDEEMED.` · `CALLED BY NAME: THOU ART MINE.` · `NOT IF, BUT WHEN.` · `A PEOPLE, AND EACH PERSON.` · then, large: `I HAVE CALLED THEE BY THY NAME.`

segments.voice: Say your own name silently, the one people who love you use, and notice how it feels, maybe tender, maybe awkward, maybe heavy with what others have said in that tone. Say it again slowly, as if spoken by someone who made you and isn't disappointed, and let the next words follow: fear not. Let them rest on whatever you're passing through right now, and if you pray, simply listen.
Jacob. The name God calls by, alongside Israel, in Isaiah forty-three's word to the exiles: created, formed, redeemed, and named. Fear not; you are mine.
Your line: you are mine. Belonging, the way a child belongs. Day four hundred sixty-nine.
